description_full: Dana Incorporated, together with its subsidiaries, provides power-conveyance and energy-management solutions for on-highway vehicles in North America, Europe, South America, and the Asia Pacific. The Light Vehicle segment provides axles, driveshafts, internal combustion engine (ICE), hybrid and electric transmissions, e-axle and e-transmission systems, inverters, electric motors, controllers, sealing and thermal products, e-sealing, e-thermal cooling systems, battery and electronics cooling, hydrogen fuel cell cooling, and new power industrial cooling. The Commercial Vehicle segment offers axles, driveshafts, hybrid and electric transmissions, e-axle and e-transmission systems, inverters, electric motors, controllers. The company offers electrodynamic technologies comprising motors, inverters, software and control systems, battery-management systems, and fuel cell plates. The company also provides sealing solutions, such as gaskets, seals, cam covers, and oil pan modules; thermal-management technologies, including transmission and engine oil cooling, battery and electronics cooling, charge air cooling, and thermal-acoustical protective shielding; and digital solutions that include active and passive system controls, as well as descriptive and predictive analytics. It serves vehicle manufacturers in the global light vehicle, medium/heavy vehicle. The company was formerly known as Dana Holding Corporation and changed its name to Dana Incorporated in August 2016. Dana Incorporated was founded in 1904 and is headquartered in Maumee, Ohio.

financial_summary: Dana Incorporated is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $2.4B market cap on $7.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -10% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 4% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $298M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 6.02× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.6× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 0.8× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 29.5% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 36% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 23% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 40% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 45% and a beta of 1.28, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.75 vs 5y 1.45), so read it loosely.

Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 221% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 12.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.7% (vs the 8% bar).

prof: ROIC of 4% falls short of the cost of capital of 7.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.70).
It converts 4% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 10% is amplified by 9.3x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 1.4% of revenue on R&D and 0.5% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 5.6x net debt to EBITDA ($469.0M of cash against $3.2B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 0.8x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.35 in the distress zone.

growth: Revenue has compounded at -9.6% over 3 years, 1.1% over 5 years and 2.2% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 37.8% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (2.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 5, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.6%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 29.5% a year to shareholders (27.2% in buybacks and 2.0% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 6.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.

CEO pay is $1.7M (6x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
